slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “John put John’s hat on John’s head.” — the name John is repeated too many times.
It is better to say:  “John put his hat on his head.”
The word his is used in place of the noun John’s.
A word used in place of a noun is called a Pronoun — the word means “instead of a noun.”

slides.text: A Pronoun is a word used instead of a noun.
examples: I, you, we  ·  him, her, them

slides.heading: Adjective Elements
bullets: An Adjective Element is a word or group of words that modifies a noun.
Adjectives and articles are adjective elements:  small lakes, the boy.
So are possessives (John’s hat) and appositives (Nero the emperor).
Anything that describes, points out, or limits a noun is an adjective element.

slides.heading: The Possessive
bullets: A Possessive is a noun or pronoun used to modify another noun by showing ownership.
“John’s hat” — John’s tells whose hat it is.
The apostrophe ( ’ ) marks a noun as a possessive:  John’s, the dog’s.
A possessive is said to be in the possessive case.
Sometimes it shows kind or authorship instead of ownership:  Ray’s Algebra.

slides.heading: Apostrophe Rules for Possessives
bullets: One owner — add ’s:  John’s hat, the ox’s horn, Moses’s slate.
More than one, ending in s — add just the apostrophe:  the ladies’ car, the boys’ coats.
More than one, not ending in s — add ’s:  the men’s farms, the children’s shoes.
A group with “of” can replace a possessive:  the nest of the bird = the bird’s nest.

slides.heading: The Appositive
bullets: An Appositive is a word or group placed beside a noun to name the same object.
It usually tells the rank, office, or business:  “Milton the poet,” “Mr. Jones the mason.”
The appositive and the noun name one and the same thing.
Set an appositive off with commas:  “Stephenson, the engineer, lived in England.”

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Appositive
slides.instruction: Name the appositive in each sentence.
items: Mr. Whitcomb the lawyer is out of town.
Whang, the Chinese miller, acted foolishly.
Stephenson, the celebrated engineer, lived in England.
Washington, the capital of the United States, is on the Potomac.
Nero, the cruel emperor, was hated.
answers: the capital of the United States

slides.heading: Personal Pronouns & the Three Persons
bullets: A Personal Pronoun shows, by its form, the person it stands for.
First Person — the speaker:  I, we.
Second Person — the one spoken to:  you  (older: thou, ye).
Third Person — the one spoken of:  he, she, it, they.
Ex. — “I write” (speaker), “you read” (spoken to), “they study” (spoken of).

slides.heading: Practice — Which Person?
slides.instruction: Tell the person of each pronoun: first, second, or third.

slides.text: A Possessive Pronoun stands for both the owner and the thing owned.
examples: This house is ours.  (ours = our house)
That book is mine.  (mine = my book)
mine, thine, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs

slides.heading: Possessive Pronoun or Possessive Adjective?
bullets: “That book is his.” — his stands alone for “his book”: a possessive pronoun.
“That is his book.” — his modifies “book”: a possessive adjective.
Stand-alone forms:  mine, thine, hers, ours, yours, theirs.
Noun-modifying forms:  my, thy, her, our, your, their.
Test — does the word stand alone (pronoun) or lean on a noun (adjective)?
